ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Psychiatry Consultation — Elizabeth I

code.originalText: Two-week review of results, diagnosis of major depression, start of treatment, and geriatric psychiatry consultation

text.paragraph: Low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and 6 percent weight loss over three months in a 69-year-old woman after several bereavements, with PHQ-9 17, GDS-15 10, and a passive death wish. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on treatment suited to an older adult and on her safety. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within two weeks; passive death wish without intent or plan, with a safety plan in place. [S]

list.item: Do you confirm a major depressive episode, as distinct from grief, and are there bipolar, psychotic, or cognitive features?
Which antidepressant, starting dose, and titration do you advise at 69, with low weight and a recent fall?
Which psychotherapy do you recommend, given her bereavements and her need for privacy?
Do you agree with the suicide-risk assessment and the safety plan?
How should her insomnia be treated now that diphenhydramine has stopped?
How long should treatment continue, and what would make you want to see her again?

text.paragraph: Ms. Tudor is seen at the request of Dr. Ashcombe-Nwosu, two weeks after her first visit, at the end of the clinic day at her request. She describes three months of a heavy, unremitting low mood that does not lift with good news, loss of pleasure in music, riding, and company, waking at 2 or 3 in the morning, poor appetite with weight loss, slowed thinking, and a sense that she has outlived her circle. She dwells on a former protégé and confidant who died two years ago after a bitter breach, and on her own part in it, with guilt that comes in waves. She has had no period of elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, or racing thoughts, and no hallucinations or fixed false beliefs. The passive wish not to wake has not recurred since the first visit; she has never harmed herself. She has no memory complaints and continues to manage her papers. She stopped diphenhydramine two weeks ago and sleeps about four hours. She drinks a small glass of wine some evenings. She prefers to be treated privately and individually and is willing to take a medicine if it is explained to her. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elizabeth was born at Greenwich on 7 September 1533 (Julian calendar; 17 September 1533 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar), the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. [D]
Her mother, Anne Boleyn, was executed in 1536, when Elizabeth was two; her father, Henry VIII, reigned until 1547. [D]
She succeeded her half-sister Mary I on Mary's death in November 1558 and never married. [D]

In October 1562, aged 29, she fell ill at Hampton Court with a fever that turned to smallpox. On 15 October she wrote that a hot fever prevented her writing more; the Spanish ambassador reported that she lost her speech and was thought lost, that the eruption appeared in the night, and that she then improved. The court feared for the succession, and she recovered. [D]

Lady Sidney, who nursed her through the smallpox, caught it and was scarred for life; the court chronology states that, unlike the Queen, she was scarred. A medal struck for the Queen's recovery shows her face unblemished. [D]
A German visitor who saw her at Greenwich in August 1598, in her 65th year, described her face as fair but wrinkled and her teeth as black, a defect he attributed to the English use of sugar. [D]
On 25 February 1601 (Julian) the Earl of Essex, once her favourite, was executed at the Tower after his rising. [D]
Through 1602 court letters describe an ache in her arm that later spread to her side and hip; in September observers wrote that her health was very good and that she hunted and rode often. [D]
In December 1602 (Julian) she strained her foot leaving a dinner at her secretary's new house and, refusing help, stumbled and fell entering her barge, bruising her shins, which soon healed. [D]

On 27 December 1602 (Julian), her godson Sir John Harington wrote that she now bore show of human infirmity: he had found her in a most pitiable state, she wept at the memory of the Irish war in which he had served with the Earl of Essex, she said she was past her relish for his verses, and she told him that her bodily meat did not suit her and that she had eaten only one ill-tasted cake since the night before. [D]

list.item: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate (F32.1). A major depressive episode of moderate severity in the setting of bereavement. Grief is present and is expected to need its own work, but the pervasive low mood, loss of pleasure, weight loss, slowed thinking, and death wish meet criteria for major depression rather than grief alone. No bipolar or psychotic features; no evidence of a neurocognitive disorder; normal tests exclude common medical causes. Suicide risk is low to moderate: older age, living without a partner, bereavement, and a recent passive death wish, set against faith, duty, close household staff, no firearms, controlled access to medicines, and good engagement. [S]
Chronic insomnia comorbid with depression (G47.00). Sleep-maintenance insomnia driven largely by the depression; diphenhydramine was rightly stopped. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: The intake history and safety plan; PHQ-9 17 at intake and 16 today; GDS-15 10; MoCA 27; hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, MCV 92 fL, white cells and platelets normal; sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.74 mg/dL, eGFR 88, glucose 88 mg/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL; TSH 2.1 mIU/L; vitamin B12 410 pg/mL; folate 9.8 ng/mL; today's vital signs and weight (52.1 kg). [S]

list.item: Sertraline 25 mg each morning for one week, then 50 mg; review every two to four weeks and increase to 75 mg, then 100 mg if needed, only if the PHQ-9 has not fallen by at least 50 percent after six to eight weeks at 50 mg. [S]
Avoid paroxetine, tricyclic antidepressants, and other strongly anticholinergic drugs; mirtazapine is a reasonable second choice if appetite and sleep fail to improve on sertraline. [S]

Check sodium two to four weeks after starting sertraline, and again with any confusion, nausea, or unsteadiness; check orthostatic blood pressure and gait after starting and after dose changes, because SSRIs raise fall risk. [S]
Individual interpersonal psychotherapy weekly, focused on grief and on the breach with her friend, combined with the antidepressant; group therapy is not suitable given her need for privacy. [S]

I agree with the risk assessment and safety plan: review suicidal thoughts at every visit with PHQ-9 item 9 and the C-SSRS Since Last Visit, keep the 988 Lifeline and clinic number on the plan, and keep her medicines with her maid. [S]
Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, with a sleep window and stimulus control; no benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines. [S]
PHQ-9 and GDS-15 at least monthly; aim for remission and continue sertraline for at least six to twelve months after remission before a slow taper. [S]
Please refer back if there is no response by about twelve weeks, if suicidal thoughts return or become active, if psychotic features or cognitive decline appear, or if she stops eating. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Ashcombe-Nwosu the same day; Ms. Tudor agrees with the plan and asked that this note be shared with no one outside her care team. [S]
Follow-up: Primary care continues with Dr. Ashcombe-Nwosu, with monthly measurement-based review. Geriatric psychiatry will see her again if needed, as above. [S]
